statement: Being creative about where you get performance boosts (e.g. using the API server's own memory as a cache) is really important.
detail: Said while introducing local API-server caching as an underappreciated startup hack.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It just that being creative in getting the performance boost is really important.

statement: System design in the real world is interesting because it makes you think at every possible step, and you should always do so: use your own reasoning at every step instead of taking components for granted.
detail: Said right after the disk-as-cache optimization, as the general lesson behind it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: system design in real world is very interesting because it helps. It makes you think at every possible step

statement: Short polling and long polling are described as (kind of) stateless patterns, in contrast to WebSockets, which keep a persistent connection.
detail: Said as the transition from long polling to WebSockets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we talk about kind of stateless short polling and long polling. Another one is WebSockets

statement: A database wire protocol (dialect) is a byte-level specification for how a query is laid out on the persistent TCP connection, e.g. first byte is X, next four bytes Y, next hundred bytes the SQL query, next five bytes Z; the 1-2 KB SQL query has to be structured according to that specification.
detail: Given while answering which protocol app servers use to talk to the database (MySQL dialect).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First byte is this, next four byte is this, next hundred byte is SQL query, next five bytes is this, right? That is a specification.

statement: Vercel, Netlify and similar tools used server-sent events for streaming deployment logs, but they have since switched their model; deployment log streaming with rich user experience in most tools still shows SSE in action.
detail: Caveat to the SSE deployment-log example (K2-135).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They leveraged this. They used to leverage it. Now they switched their model

statement: With SNS plus SQS you can replicate the behaviour where multiple consumers receive the same messages.
detail: Student 1's lead-in to the SQS-to-Kinesis war story (K3-012); follows the teacher's point that SNS+SQS can mimic Kafka (K3-008). Not separately confirmed by the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: with SNS and SQS, we can replicate the behavior where like multiple consumers can actually have the same messages.

statement: In the student's multi-level config cache, if in-memory data is flushed, reads fall back to the local disk copy; this disk path is always exercised anyway because memory is empty when the application starts.
detail: Teacher probed: 'is it possible in your case that memory is flushed?' Student: it falls back to disk, and that path is always covered on start-up. Teacher: 'Pretty interesting.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: let's say if if it is flushed then you know it will fall back to disk.

statement: The teacher has used SQS very widely.
detail: Said while pointing out that visibility-timeout equivalents exist in RabbitMQ and Google Pub/Sub.
speaker: teacher

statement: For SSE-based features, testing the business logic for each type of message received is enough; you can rely on the connection itself, because it will be functional anyway.
detail: Teacher's justification for never unit-testing the SSE connection itself (see K3-086).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: never tested the connection, but I've tested what I received on the connection. Right. So you can rely on that anyway
